{{short description|American mathematician and inventor}}
'''Raymond Moos Redheffer''' (April 17, 1921 – May 13, 2005)<ref name="gamelin">{{citation|url=http://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/_files/inmemoriam/html/raymondredheffer.htm|title=In Memoriam: Raymond Redheffer|publisher=University of California Senate|first=Theodore W.|last=Gamelin|author-link=Theodore Gamelin|year=2005}}.</ref> was an American [[mathematician]] and inventor. He was the creator of one of the first electronic games, [[Nim]], a knowledge game.<ref>[http://gameshow.com.br/?p=10447 A História dos Games - A origem (1942-1961)]</ref>

== Early life ==
From 1939 to 1950, Redheffer was an undergraduate and graduate student at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] and as a Pierce Fellow at Harvard. While in graduate school, he worked at the [[MIT Radiation Laboratory|Radiation Laboratory]], a [[WW II]] research laboratory developing [[radar]], and the [[Research Laboratory of Electronics]], which were both part of [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]. He taught as a [[Benjamin Peirce]] Fellow at [[Harvard]] from 1948 to 1950.<ref name="gamelin" /> He earned his PhD in 1948 from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology under [[Norman Levinson]].{{efn|He and Levinson would later write the 1970 book ''Complex Variable''.{{cite book |author2=Levinson |first1=Norman |author1=Redheffer, Raymond |title=Complex Variables |date=1970 |publisher=Holden-Day |isbn=978-0-07-037492-8}}}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Redheffer |first=Raymond |date=1969 |title=The Homotopy Theorems of Function Theory |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2317866 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=76 |issue=7 |pages=778–787 |doi=10.2307/2317866 |issn=0002-9890}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1949, Redheffer and co-inventors Edward B. McMillan and Herbert Leaderman applied for a patent for a [[dielectric]] wall for the transmission of [[microwave radiation]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=November 17, 1953 |title=Dielectric walls for transmission of centrimetric radiation. Patent # 2,659,884 |url=https://ppubs.uspto.gov/api/pdf/downloadPdf/US-2659884-A?source=USOCR&requestToken=eyJzdWIiOiJjYjZlMDU1ZS04NjhiLTQ2MDMtYjNiMy1lMjlhMWRhNDYwMjYiLCJ2ZXIiOiIxNWJmZDU5MS0xNTZjLTQ1ZDItOTZjMy01MzFiYWQ5MTk2YjMiLCJleHAiOjB9}}</ref> In 1950, Redheffer began teaching mathematics at UCLA.<ref name="gamelin" /> In 1953, he was awarded the patent for a computer for evaluating complex integrals.<ref>{{Cite web |title=U.S. Patent Office, 24646497, Computer for evaluating complex integrals |url=https://ppubs.uspto.gov/api/patents/html/US-2638268-A?source=USPAT&requestToken=eyJzdWIiOiI3NjdlNWQ3YS02ZTEyLTQ2YTgtOWY1YS1lNTNkYTA5ODFiMTEiLCJ2ZXIiOiI2M2FlYTAwOC02ZDFhLTQ3ZjktYjU0Mi1hNzFlNTBiMmRiYzUiLCJleHAiOjB9}}</ref> Later that year, he was awarded a patent for a computing machine. Both [[Transfer (patent)|patents were assigned]] to the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy.]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=United State Patent Office: 2,656,102, COMPUTING MACHINE |url=https://ppubs.uspto.gov/api/pdf/downloadPdf/US-2656102-A?source=USPAT&requestToken=eyJzdWIiOiJlNmZiNjgwOC1iZTI1LTRjN2QtYmZhYy04YjhkNGMwMThlY2IiLCJ2ZXIiOiI3MjIwODEyNC1mZGJmLTRkNWItYTYxMi1jNzUxODY1ZTQzYmUiLCJleHAiOjB9}}</ref><ref>{{Cite patent|number=US2638268A|title=Computer for evaluating complex integrals|gdate=1953-05-12|invent1=Redheffer|inventor1-first=Raymond M.|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US2638268A/en?q=(raymond+redheffer)&oq=raymond+redheffer}}</ref> In November of that same year, Redheffer, McMillan, and Leaderman were awarded the 1953 patent for their 1949 dielectric patent application, with the patent assigned to McMillan<ref name=":1" /> In the world of mathematics, Redheffer would later be known for the [[Redheffer star product]] which he had introduced in 1959.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Redheffer |first=Raymond |date=1959 |title=Inequalities for a Matrix Riccati Equation |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24900576 |journal=Journal of Mathematics and Mechanics |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=349–367 |issn=0095-9057}}</ref> Redheffer and McMillan were awarded a 1960 patent for another dielectric wall application, this for a more generalized application, which was a dielectric wall for transmission of [[electromagnetic radiation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=U.S. Patent Office, 2,956,281, DIELECTRIC WALLS FOR TRANSMISSION OF ELECTROMAGNETIC RADIATION |url=https://ppubs.uspto.gov/api/pdf/downloadPdf/US-2956281-A?source=USPAT&requestToken=eyJzdWIiOiI3NjdlNWQ3YS02ZTEyLTQ2YTgtOWY1YS1lNTNkYTA5ODFiMTEiLCJ2ZXIiOiI2M2FlYTAwOC02ZDFhLTQ3ZjktYjU0Mi1hNzFlNTBiMmRiYzUiLCJleHAiOjB9}}</ref>

In 1961, he collaborated with [[Charles Eames]] on a series of animated short films about mathematics for the exhibition at the [[California Museum of Science and Industry]] in [[Los Angeles]]. He later worked and with Eames on his 1966 [[timeline of mathematics]] entitled ''[[Men of Modern Mathematics]]'' which was printed and distributed by [[IBM]].<ref name="gamelin" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Mathematica: A World of Numbers . . . and Beyond |url=https://www.eamesoffice.com/the-work/mathematica/ |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=Eames Office |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Alpha |url=https://eamesfoundation.org/work/alpha/ |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=Eames Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> In that same year, notable and unusual is the physically motivated discussion of the functions of [[vector calculus]] in his book with [[Ivan S. Sokolnikoff|Ivan Sokolnikoff]], ''Mathematics of Physics and Modern Engineering'' (1966).<ref>Sokolnikoff, Ivan Stephen; Redheffer, Raymond M. (1966). ''Mathematics of Physics and Modern Engineering''. McGraw-Hill. {{ISBN|978-0-07-059625-2}}</ref>  Eleven years later, his paper ''An explicitly solvable optimization task'' (1977) was the source for what is now the [[Redheffer matrix]] and was also a notable mathematical achievement.<ref>{{Citation |last=Redheffer |first=Ray |chapter=Eine explizit lösbare Optimierungsaufgabe |date=1977 |title=Numerische Methoden bei Optimierungsaufgaben Band 3: Optimierung bei graphentheoretischen und ganzzahligen Problemen |pages=213–216 |editor-last=Collatz |editor-first=L. |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-0348-5936-3_13 |access-date=2026-07-15 |place=Basel |publisher=Birkhäuser |language=de |doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-5936-3_13 |isbn=978-3-0348-5936-3 |editor2-last=Meinardus |editor2-first=G. |editor3-last=Wetterling |editor3-first=W.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

His teaching skills were acknowledged 6 decades later by one of his students.<ref>Seligman, Stephen J. (2009) Precepts for Freshmen, The Harvard Crimson September 2</ref> He taught for 55 years at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]],<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=17822}}</ref> writing more than 200 research papers, ranging from microwave analysis and dielectric constants, and three textbooks.<ref name="gamelin" /> He may have invented a version of [[Nim]] with electronic components.

== Recognition ==

* UCLA Distinguished Teaching Award (1969).

== Filmography ==
Films created by Redheffer and the [[Eames Office]]:

* '''''Alpha'' (1972)''', 1 minute, 16 seconds [[Stop motion|stop-motion]] animated color film on [[algebraic expressions]].<ref name=":0" />
* '''''Two Laws of Algebra: Distributive & Associative'' (1972)''', 4 minute animated film. Music by [[Laurindo Almeida]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Two Laws of Algebra: Distributive & Associative |url=https://eamesfoundation.org/work/two-laws-of-algebra-distributive-associative/ |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=Eames Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref>
* '''''Exponents: A Study in Generalization'' (1972), a''' short animated film.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ray Eames Shapes & Colors–Math Film Animation {{!}} Eames Institute |url=https://www.eamesinstitute.org/collection/artifacts/mathematical-film-study-material-1/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260308211828/https://www.eamesinstitute.org/collection/artifacts/mathematical-film-study-material-1/ |archive-date=2026-03-08 |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=www.eamesinstitute.org |language=en}}</ref>
